sources.title: The legacy of Wangari Maathai continues

facts.text: When Maathai learned in 2004 that she had won the Nobel Peace Prize, she went outside and planted a tree.
Maathai was born in 1940 in Nyeri, Kenya, to a farming family in the highlands of Mount Kenya.
She studied biology in the United States before returning to Kenya.
She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, and she taught at the University of Nairobi.
Her first aim was to help poor rural women who lacked clean water and wood for fires.
In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, which taught women to plant trees on farms and around schools and churches.
The trees helped keep water clean and provided wood, and the movement promoted sustainable livelihoods.
The movement has helped plant more than 40 million trees across Kenya.
The Kenyan government of the time regarded her as a threat; tree planting became a peaceful way to resist it and empower women.
In 2002 she was elected to Kenya’s parliament with 98 percent of the vote.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
She explained that conflicts often arise from competition over scarce or damaged resources, so managing resources responsibly supports peace.
The African Union marks March 3 as Wangari Maathai Day.
